   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not

From Ken Stearn, FIFE



Dear Outlet,

After many happy years spent
with most Spectrum models, I
have finally moved on to a "SAM"


I have been trying, without
success, to eliminate the lines
across a graphic dump with Flash
or otherwise. I tried poking
83238,27,51,n 83246,27,51,n as
suggested in a letter from Colin
Demaline in Outlet 47.My printer
is a Toshiba Express Writer 301
24-pin which recognizes standard
Epson codes.

The smallest line feeds used are
n/180" but when using "Dump" the
printer seems to lose control
(me too); this is with the
dipswitch disabled. I would very
much appreciate a Sam version of
BASDUMP, which you wrote for the
Spectrum, or the way to rewrite
it.

                    Ken Stearn

   BRIAN CAVERS TO KEN STEARN
I find no Epson code for n/180"
line feed as you state but FLASH
uses the standard Epson 8/72"
(equals 20/180").If your printer
code for n/180" is 3 bytes long
(with ESC code, usually 27),it
can be POKEd over the 8/72"codes
thus... POKE 83238,n,n,n  and...
POKE 83246,n,n,n  ...where n,n,n
are the 3 codes used by your
printer for 20/180" linefeed. If
LESS than 3 bytes are used,put a
0 as the last byte.Obviously I
can't test it so let me know how
you get on.

A BASIC graphic dump,GEEDEE, was
in Issue 33 if you want to exp-
eriment. It could be improved if
speed is unimportant.
                        - Brian

From Brian Gaff, SURREY



Since the news that CP/M is
available for the SAM was made
public on the Hotline, I have
received many calls from people
who seem to know nothing about
it! Perhaps I could use this
spot to clarify a few things.


Firstly, I must make it clear
that our product - Pro-Dos - is
not in any way connected with
Digital Research, who own the
rights to the CP/M name, and
code. No, Pro-Dos is a CP/M 2.2
compatible system.

The idea behind CP/M was to
create a standard interface, or
bridge if you like,between mach-
ines and their software. The way
this was done was to detail all
the functions that would be re-
quired by software, and to give
each standard entry and exit
parameters, and call addresses.
Now the actual routines could be
anywhere, depending on machine;
all that was required was that a
jumpblock existed in the same
locations in all the machines.

Of course there is more to it
than that, but it gives you the
general idea. The main reason
for implementing it on SAM was
to gain access to the vast
amount of PD software that has
been written for the system.

We hope to help out by sourcing
some of the PD as well as giving
advice on where commercial
programs can be obtained, and
converting from other disc
formats.


The Pro-Dos disc format is not
the SAM format as, for technical
reasons, this would not work.
However, we have used the format
seen on the Amstrad PCW B:
drive, which makes conversion
fairly easy.

Finally, a word about those
involved in the rather long job
of producing, what is in effect,
a completely new operating
system, and debugging it.

Pro-Dos was written by Chris
Pile, who you will probably have
heard of, if you are a regular
OUTLET reader [More so in the
Spectrum version - BC] So far he
has had little reward for his
efforts, but hopefully that will
change soon!

I must also thank Wayne Weedon
for his help in showing us how
to drive the SAM hardware, and
his work on configuring the PD
software etc.

Some may think CP/M is boring,
with no graphics, and 80-column
screen, but if you want to use
your SAM for serious tasks, then
the abundance of cheap software
is very welcome.

On to another SAM-related tack
now. As you may recall, our
original intention was to get
comms going on SAM. To do this,
we had two approaches in mind.
The first was to just provide
software to drive a modem from
the Comms interface RS232. The
second, was to make an interface
so that the old Spectrum modem,
the VTX5000, could be used.

The second option was not taken
up, as we had little interest. I
think most users wanted to use
faster, more modern modems to
keep the phone bills down!

We have, however, run into a
snag. It seems that not all SAMs
with comms interfaces were
created equal!

With the test software we have,
we are finding that data coming
in through the RS232 can be
corrupted but not on all systems
or all of the time!

In an effort to find out how
widespead problems are, could I
ask any reader who has played
around bringing data in through
the comms RS232, to let us know
how they got on? It would be
rather a shame if we started
selling software that only some
users could get to work! At
present we think it is being
caused by interference getting
to the UART chip via the power
supply.

                 Brian

From Reg Jeffs, WOOLWICH

Is there a possibility of prod-
ucing a program for the SAM like
you did on the Spectrum that is,
putting machine code in a REM?

                   Reg Jeffs

I've gone off the idea a little
bit on SAM because the BASIC may
crash(when editing NEAR the REM)
but in this issue is "CODESTORE"
which has REMs in which you can
at least store a character set
(768 bytes) and UDGs(168 bytes)
as well as a routine to store a
SCREEN$ in memory and display it
as needed. "UNPOKE",in Issue 51,
is also worth considering for
short bits of code.
                        - Brian

From: S.W. Greenwood,N.YORKSHIRE

Dear Sir,

Since receiving my batch of
OUTLETS I have not had time to
evaluate them in depth but I am
impressed with what I have seen
so far; a very professional
presentation.

I recently received a batch of
second-hand microdrive cart-
ridges which I bought through
MicroMart. Some were blank but
one had September '91 OUTLET on,
albeit somewhat corrupted. I
managed to read the letters
feature and I noted an enquiry
about a PAL programmer for the
Spectrum.

Your reply also stated that you
didn't really unerstand the
question and asked for clarifi-
cation; here it is.

PAL stands for Programmable
Logic Array and is, as its name
implies, an integrated circuit
with a number of logic gates
forming an array. To use this to
implement a logic function one
needs to program it by blowing
fuses, which are Links with the
chip. One keeps the Links one
needs and blows the Links one
does not need.

It belongs in the same family of
devices as the ULA (uncommitted
Logic Array) whose name, in view
of the previous remarks,is self-
explanatory.

It is a block of generalised
logic which,in its virgin state,
is uncommitted to any particular
function.It needs to be program-
med to perform a specific task.
These devices can replace a
whole batch of gates and flip-
flops, and bring a measure of
programmability into discrete
logic design.


I hope that this clarifies the
matter for you. It is a subject
I know a deal about as I am an
electronics design engineer, and
I spent many years designing
circuits and systems for
electronic control in automation
and instrumentation.

I am now unemployed and, because
I am almost retiring age,that is
not likely to change. However, I
keep myself amused and my brain
in gear with my Spectrum.


It started out as 16k but has
now got 48k, a proper keyboard,
and a proper PSU, which are the
two areas where corners were
cut. With those points taken
care of, I find it a very useful
machine indeed. In addition, I
use Betabasic which transforms
it into a first class unit.

I use it to play with Z80 code,
and to write programs for
circuit analysis and mathematics
which are my main interests.

Although I have been involved
with computers in one way or
another, from designing them to
using them in systems, since
1960, I had never had one of my
own until I got the Spectrum. I
have tried other machines, but
always come round to the view
that I can do everything I want
with what I've got.


To return to the PAL programmer
question,it would be technically
feasible to design one around a
Spectrum in the same way that
there have been designs for PROM
programmers but I can say with
reasonable confidence that this
has not been done as I think I
would have heard of it.

I have toyed with the idea of
producing some tutorial programs
on logic design along with a
method of simulating the logic,
therefore proving it before
building it. I thought that with
all the present-day "hype" about
IBM, and the widespread belief
among the majority that the
Spectrum is a kid's toy, that
nobody would take such a thing
seriously. However, it does seem
that there is a band of users
out there who recognise a good
thing when they see it.

        Yours sincerely,

         Stan Greenwood

Brian Cavers to Stan Greenwood

Many thanks for the explanation!
I now see a PAL is not the same
as PROM or EPROM memory;the main
difference being a PAL chip is
not blank to start with but is
pre-programmed with generalized
circuitry which is customized,as
you describe,by blowing fuses at
various places. Yes, that's new
to me and very interesting.Stick
around - your experience should
be useful to readers with hard-
ware queries - and why not share
your programs with us?

The SAM COUPE may also interest
you because Andy Wright's SAM
BASIC is BETABASIC with extra
features and the SAM is really a
"super-Spectrum".       - Brian

From: P.A. Bates, SIDCUP

Dear Ron and Brian,

You may remember I wrote to you
many issues ago about getting
work into print and the various
print options open to us.  Well,
you may have used or seen the
latest printer style on the
market - the bubble jet printer.

We have at work one of the most
sophisticated bubble jet colour
printers around. The "iris" ink
jet printer, this machine,
driven by whisper-based
mainframe computers through a
simple 286 pc gives one of the
best quality colour pre-proof
pictures I have ever seen.

The iris consists of a large
revolving drum down on which the
sub-straite, (paper to you), is
stuck and, as it spins, four ink
jets travel on a carriage along
the length of the paper. The
four inks: cyan, magenta, yellow
and black drop onto the paper or
are deflected by a shield which
moves into and out of position
many times a second.


The software which drives this
machine can,of course,be altered
to give different results for
different printing processes or
for different papers or can give
more than one copy, you can fit
about four A4 copies at one
time.

The main difference between this
ink jet system and conventional
systems is the image itself. You
may remember I told you that
images were made up of dots with
the heavier dots carrying the
most ink and appearing darker in
shade. Well, this new system has
no dots but the different shades
of colour are made by how many
times the deflector shield moves
in front of the jets and how
long it actually stays in place.

The biggest drawback is hardware
has to be kept scrupulously
clean at all times and of course
no b*!#!* ever wants to clean
it! There is so much happening
on the professional DTP front
that it is very hard to keep up
with it all.          P.A.BATES

Brian Cavers to K.P.A. Bates

Sounds good! I bet it cost a lot
though. Why not send us a sample
printout just for interest?

                        - Brian

should work. It is likely that I
introduced the fault myself when
I included our Spectrum OUTLET
printer dump routine which sets
RND to the same value every time
a card is dumped!        - Brian.

From Dave Marriott, NOTTINGHAM



Dear Ron & Brian,

I noticed that "Outwrite" sends
an Initialise Printer command
("ESC @") before printing a text
file. This gave me a bit of a
problem as I'd customised it to
allow certain printer control
codes to be sent from the User
Basic menu, and the "ESC @"
wiped 'em out! After a bit of
prodding around, I managed to
come up with a Poke to suppress
the "ESC @", which might be
helpful to anyone doing similar
things...

 Load "Outwrite" disc in drive 1
 CLEAR 65535
 LOAD "wordcd2" CODE
 POKE 71915,0,0,0,0,0,0
 SAVE OVER "wordcd2" CODE
 65536,16384
Of course you have to make sure
the printer is "initialised"
yourself or send your own"ESC @"
BEFORE your control codes and it
is a good idea to save the orig-
inal "wordcd2" somewhere safe
before tinkering with it, just
in case!
                  Dave Marriott


Thanks, Dave. The whole thing
will also be revised in the
upgrade version in the light of
feedback from readers.
                        - Brian

From:Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER

Dear Brian and Ron,

A thought occured to me about
you having problems with some of
my discs on your SAM. The one
disc I now remember was not
formatted on SAM it was origin-
ally done on the Disciple.

This could well have been part
of the problem although I have
not noticed it this end and any
disc formatted on any system
works on any other here.

Still I have things a bit more
organised, not a lot!! but now
have discs formatted for their
proper systems.

My replacement drive from SAMCO
is (so far, fingers crossed) a
lot better and the problem of
failing to format discs has gone
away.I'm now even more convinced
it was a suspect drive and that
the head for side 2 was not
writing to disc reliably.

COLOUR DUMPS. One of the
criticisms I made about both the
one from PBT and the one on the
ENCELADUS disc was that after
entering in all the colour set-
up data there was no provision
to SAVE it for future use. In
both cases this can be overcome.
Enceladus program:when you enter
the data writes it into BASIC
lines using the KEYIN function
(Writes BASIC lines starting
598).

All you have to do after enter-
ing data is to BREAK and SAVE
the whole of the BASIC program.
The MC section is held in REM
statement so is SAVEd as well.
You have in effect a self-
contained customised program. To
restart, RUN START (RETURN) or
for auto run SAVE "name" LINE
5140.This SAVE option could be
added to the program for ease
between 6260/ 6270 to add an
additional menu option to the
"end, next, more".

PBT program "pokes" the data
into memory locations 16726 to
16757 so a few BASIC lines could
be added to SAVE this section of
memory or alternatively SAVE the
whole MC routine as a customised
version.

You then need to add the option
to either LOAD the code block or
customised MC back into the pro-
gram.Lines 350/360 look a likely
place to add the LOAD (at change
colour option) and also for SAVE
as this point is returned to
after a change sequence.

Since having OUTWRITE I've used
roll paper most of the time so
have not noticed a problem with
sheet paper before - that after
doing a print,removing paper and
then pressing "N" for "another
copy?" the program seems to lock
up because with the LC10 if no
paper in printer it goes off
line automatically and cannot be
put back on until more paper is
loaded. (Other printers are
probably the same).

The text editor can be re-
entered with the ESC key. Would
it be possible to avoid this
totally by eliminating the LF
after the "N" for another copy?
and send the LF at the end of
printing and before the"another"
prompt.

Selecting drive: I have modified
the program so as to use the
following form.(so far only in
the SAVE sequence but could be
added to MERGE and LOAD file if
required).

"name" normal SAVE to current
drive

"1name" makes d1 current and
SAVEs "name" to drive 1

"2name" makes d2 current & SAVEs
"name" to drive 2

"1" makes d1 current  (without a
SAVE)

"2" makes d2 current  (without a
SaVe)

This avoids having a seperate
"select drive" option.

The choice of 1 or 2 SAVEs
automaticly has also been added.

"name" is one SAVE

"name+" SAVEs "name1" then
"name2"  (automaticly adds
suffix 1 & 2)

The disc change is still valid
with the double SAVE i.e.
"2name+" This is done with
(relatively) simple mods to
BASIC. However, no doubt there
will be lots of "unoficial" mods
and the "official" upgrade will
be totally different. Just
happens to suit my needs.

Incidently the SAVE prompts now
show current drive and after a
SAVE sequence asks if further
SAVEs are required (just the
thing for writing 20 scrolling
screens to OUTLET, two SAVEs to
disc to send off and a couple to
the backup in case the G.P.O.
loses the first).If you have a
bad memory further SAVEs tell
you the last file name used.

MASTERDOS: The speed of the
MASTERDOS "BACKUP" means it is
used quite often even for
Disciple +D discs. No problem
copying +D discs with Masterdos,
well almost no problem! Files 2
to 80 are true +D copies. First
file is not. After a copy by
this method it will load as LOAD
"name" but not as LOAD P1.

This is because MASTERDOS writes
the disc name into P1 file
position towards the end of the
sector map (if no name is used
it writes "spaces" char 32)and
thus overwrites the file data
needed by the Disciple to find
the file by "P" method. It seems
the Disciple does not need this
data for "name" method.

If the SYS is the first one on
disc it still BOOTs O.K.and it's
not very often the SYS code is
loaded by LOAD Px.The problem is
only noticed if other files
happen to be at P1. BACKUP is
still the fastest option to
"backup" Disciple discs but the
file at position 1 needs to be
reSAVEd using Disciple COPY to
get the header back to normal.
If a lot of copying is done a
routine could be used to do a
"backup" followed by a TRACK 0,
Sec 1 copy which will also re-
store things. Remember "backup"
is a form of FORMAT 1 TO 2 and
has no regard for what's already
on the disc.

          Malcolm Perry

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Perry

As far as disc-reliability, one
of the things we are now trying
is to increase the step-rate.
Paul Thomas of PBT thought the
default rate of 3 milliseconds
was pushing the SAM drives to

From Brian Gaff, SURREY

Since the news that CP/M is available for the SAM was made public on the Hotline, I have received many calls from people who seem to know nothing about it! Perhaps I could use this spot to clarify a few things.

Firstly, I must make it clear that our product - Pro-Dos - is not in any way connected with Digital Research, who own the rights to the CP/M name, and code. No, Pro-Dos is a CP/M 2.2 compatible system.

The idea behind CP/M was to create a standard interface, or bridge if you like,between mach- ines and their software. The way this was done was to detail all the functions that would be re- quired by software, and to give each standard entry and exit parameters, and call addresses. Now the actual routines could be anywhere, depending on machine; all that was required was that a jumpblock existed in the same locations in all the machines.

Of course there is more to it than that, but it gives you the general idea. The main reason for implementing it on SAM was to gain access to the vast amount of PD software that has been written for the system.

We hope to help out by sourcing some of the PD as well as giving advice on where commercial programs can be obtained, and converting from other disc formats.

The Pro-Dos disc format is not the SAM format as, for technical reasons, this would not work. However, we have used the format seen on the Amstrad PCW B: drive, which makes conversion fairly easy.

Finally, a word about those involved in the rather long job of producing, what is in effect, a completely new operating system, and debugging it.

Pro-Dos was written by Chris Pile, who you will probably have heard of, if you are a regular OUTLET reader [More so in the Spectrum version - BC] So far he has had little reward for his efforts, but hopefully that will change soon!

I must also thank Wayne Weedon for his help in showing us how to drive the SAM hardware, and his work on configuring the PD software etc.

Some may think CP/M is boring, with no graphics, and 80-column screen, but if you want to use your SAM for serious tasks, then the abundance of cheap software is very welcome.

On to another SAM-related tack now. As you may recall, our original intention was to get comms going on SAM. To do this, we had two approaches in mind. The first was to just provide software to drive a modem from the Comms interface RS232. The second, was to make an interface so that the old Spectrum modem, the VTX5000, could be used.

The second option was not taken up, as we had little interest. I think most users wanted to use faster, more modern modems to keep the phone bills down!

We have, however, run into a snag. It seems that not all SAMs with comms interfaces were created equal!

With the test software we have, we are finding that data coming in through the RS232 can be corrupted but not on all systems or all of the time!

In an effort to find out how widespead problems are, could I ask any reader who has played around bringing data in through the comms RS232, to let us know how they got on? It would be rather a shame if we started selling software that only some users could get to work! At present we think it is being caused by interference getting to the UART chip via the power supply.

Brian

Since receiving my batch of OUTLETS I have not had time to evaluate them in depth but I am impressed with what I have seen so far; a very professional presentation.

Your reply also stated that you didn't really unerstand the question and asked for clarifi- cation; here it is.

PAL stands for Programmable Logic Array and is, as its name implies, an integrated circuit with a number of logic gates forming an array. To use this to implement a logic function one needs to program it by blowing fuses, which are Links with the chip. One keeps the Links one needs and blows the Links one does not need.

It belongs in the same family of devices as the ULA (uncommitted Logic Array) whose name, in view of the previous remarks,is self- explanatory.

It is a block of generalised logic which,in its virgin state, is uncommitted to any particular function.It needs to be program- med to perform a specific task. These devices can replace a whole batch of gates and flip- flops, and bring a measure of programmability into discrete logic design.

I hope that this clarifies the matter for you. It is a subject I know a deal about as I am an electronics design engineer, and I spent many years designing circuits and systems for electronic control in automation and instrumentation.

I am now unemployed and, because I am almost retiring age,that is not likely to change. However, I keep myself amused and my brain in gear with my Spectrum.

It started out as 16k but has now got 48k, a proper keyboard, and a proper PSU, which are the two areas where corners were cut. With those points taken care of, I find it a very useful machine indeed. In addition, I use Betabasic which transforms it into a first class unit.

I use it to play with Z80 code, and to write programs for circuit analysis and mathematics which are my main interests.

Although I have been involved with computers in one way or another, from designing them to using them in systems, since 1960, I had never had one of my own until I got the Spectrum. I have tried other machines, but always come round to the view that I can do everything I want with what I've got.

To return to the PAL programmer question,it would be technically feasible to design one around a Spectrum in the same way that there have been designs for PROM programmers but I can say with reasonable confidence that this has not been done as I think I would have heard of it.

I have toyed with the idea of producing some tutorial programs on logic design along with a method of simulating the logic, therefore proving it before building it. I thought that with all the present-day "hype" about IBM, and the widespread belief among the majority that the Spectrum is a kid's toy, that nobody would take such a thing seriously. However, it does seem that there is a band of users out there who recognise a good thing when they see it.

Yours sincerely,

Stan Greenwood

You may remember I wrote to you many issues ago about getting work into print and the various print options open to us.  Well, you may have used or seen the latest printer style on the market - the bubble jet printer.

We have at work one of the most sophisticated bubble jet colour printers around. The "iris" ink jet printer, this machine, driven by whisper-based mainframe computers through a simple 286 pc gives one of the best quality colour pre-proof pictures I have ever seen.

The iris consists of a large revolving drum down on which the sub-straite, (paper to you), is stuck and, as it spins, four ink jets travel on a carriage along the length of the paper. The four inks: cyan, magenta, yellow and black drop onto the paper or are deflected by a shield which moves into and out of position many times a second.

The software which drives this machine can,of course,be altered to give different results for different printing processes or for different papers or can give more than one copy, you can fit about four A4 copies at one time.

The main difference between this ink jet system and conventional systems is the image itself. You may remember I told you that images were made up of dots with the heavier dots carrying the most ink and appearing darker in shade. Well, this new system has no dots but the different shades of colour are made by how many times the deflector shield moves in front of the jets and how long it actually stays in place.

COLOUR DUMPS. One of the criticisms I made about both the one from PBT and the one on the ENCELADUS disc was that after entering in all the colour set- up data there was no provision to SAVE it for future use. In both cases this can be overcome. Enceladus program:when you enter the data writes it into BASIC lines using the KEYIN function (Writes BASIC lines starting 598).

All you have to do after enter- ing data is to BREAK and SAVE the whole of the BASIC program. The MC section is held in REM statement so is SAVEd as well. You have in effect a self- contained customised program. To restart, RUN START (RETURN) or for auto run SAVE "name" LINE 5140.This SAVE option could be added to the program for ease between 6260/ 6270 to add an additional menu option to the "end, next, more".

PBT program "pokes" the data into memory locations 16726 to 16757 so a few BASIC lines could be added to SAVE this section of memory or alternatively SAVE the whole MC routine as a customised version.

You then need to add the option to either LOAD the code block or customised MC back into the pro- gram.Lines 350/360 look a likely place to add the LOAD (at change colour option) and also for SAVE as this point is returned to after a change sequence.

Since having OUTWRITE I've used roll paper most of the time so have not noticed a problem with sheet paper before - that after doing a print,removing paper and then pressing "N" for "another copy?" the program seems to lock up because with the LC10 if no paper in printer it goes off line automatically and cannot be put back on until more paper is loaded. (Other printers are probably the same).

The text editor can be re- entered with the ESC key. Would it be possible to avoid this totally by eliminating the LF after the "N" for another copy? and send the LF at the end of printing and before the"another" prompt.

Selecting drive: I have modified the program so as to use the following form.(so far only in the SAVE sequence but could be added to MERGE and LOAD file if required).

"name" normal SAVE to current drive

"1name" makes d1 current and SAVEs "name" to drive 1

"2name" makes d2 current & SAVEs "name" to drive 2

"1" makes d1 current  (without a SAVE)

"2" makes d2 current  (without a SaVe)

This avoids having a seperate "select drive" option.

The choice of 1 or 2 SAVEs automaticly has also been added.

"name" is one SAVE

"name+" SAVEs "name1" then "name2"  (automaticly adds suffix 1 & 2)

The disc change is still valid with the double SAVE i.e. "2name+" This is done with (relatively) simple mods to BASIC. However, no doubt there will be lots of "unoficial" mods and the "official" upgrade will be totally different. Just happens to suit my needs.

Incidently the SAVE prompts now show current drive and after a SAVE sequence asks if further SAVEs are required (just the thing for writing 20 scrolling screens to OUTLET, two SAVEs to disc to send off and a couple to the backup in case the G.P.O. loses the first).If you have a bad memory further SAVEs tell you the last file name used.

MASTERDOS: The speed of the MASTERDOS "BACKUP" means it is used quite often even for Disciple +D discs. No problem copying +D discs with Masterdos, well almost no problem! Files 2 to 80 are true +D copies. First file is not. After a copy by this method it will load as LOAD "name" but not as LOAD P1.

This is because MASTERDOS writes the disc name into P1 file position towards the end of the sector map (if no name is used it writes "spaces" char 32)and thus overwrites the file data needed by the Disciple to find the file by "P" method. It seems the Disciple does not need this data for "name" method.

Идея CP/M заключалась в создании стандартного интерфейса или, если хотите, моста между компьютерами и их программным обеспечением. Сделано это было путем детального описания всех функций, которые могут потребоваться программам, с назначением каждой стандартных входных и выходных параметров, а также адресов вызова. Сами же исполняемые подпрограммы могли находиться где угодно, в зависимости от машины; требовалось лишь, чтобы таблица переходов (jumpblock) находилась по одним и тем же адресам на всех компьютерах.

Конечно, все устроено сложнее, но это дает общее представление. Главная причина переноса системы на SAM заключалась в том, чтобы получить доступ к огромному количеству программного обеспечения Public Domain, написанного для этой платформы.

Мы надеемся помочь как с поиском некоторого PD-софта, так и с предоставлением советов о том, где можно достать коммерческие программы, а также с конвертацией с других дисковых форматов.

Формат дисков Pro-Dos не совпадает с форматом SAM, так как по техническим причинам это не сработало бы. Однако мы использовали формат, применяемый на Amstrad PCW для дисковода B:, что делает конвертацию довольно простой.

Pro-Dos была написана Chris Pile, о котором вы, вероятно, слышали, если регулярно читаете OUTLET [Особенно в версии для Spectrum — BC]. До сих пор он почти ничего не получил за свои труды, но, надеемся, скоро это изменится!

Некоторые могут счесть CP/M скучной из-за отсутствия графики и 80-колоночного текстового экрана, но если вы хотите использовать свой SAM для серьезных задач, то изобилие дешевого программного обеспечения придется весьма кстати.

Первый состоял в том, чтобы просто предоставить программное обеспечение для управления модемом через RS232 интерфейса Comms. Второй — сделать интерфейс для подключения старого модема от Spectrum, VTX5000.

В своем ответе вы также упомянули, что не совсем поняли вопрос, и попросили разъяснений; вот они.

PAL означает Programmable Logic Array (программируемая матричная логика) и представляет собой, как следует из названия, интегральную схему с набором логических вентилей, образующих матрицу. Чтобы использовать ее для реализации логической функции, ее необходимо запрограммировать путем пережигания плавких перемычек внутри чипа. Нужные перемычки сохраняются, а ненужные — пережигаются.

Этот чип относится к тому же семейству устройств, что и ULA (Uncommitted Logic Array — нескоммутированная логическая матрица), чье название с учетом сказанного говорит само за себя.

Это блок универсальной логики, который в исходном состоянии не привязан к какой-либо конкретной функции. Его необходимо запрограммировать для выполнения определенной задачи. Такие микросхемы способны заменить целую россыпь дискретных вентилей и триггеров, привнося гибкость программирования в разработку схем на дискретной логике.

Сейчас я безработный, и, поскольку я уже почти пенсионного возраста, вряд ли это изменится. Впрочем, я развлекаюсь и держу мозги в тонусе с помощью своего Spectrum.

Изначально он был 16k, но теперь у него 48k, нормальная клавиатура и нормальный блок питания — две вещи, на которых изначально сэкономили. С устранением этих недостатков машина оказалась действительно очень полезной. Кроме того, я использую Betabasic, который превращает её в первоклассный аппарат.

Я использую его, чтобы баловаться с кодом Z80 и писать программы для анализа электроцепей и математических вычислений, что и составляет мой главный интерес.
